Attorney here.

It is possible to represent oneself in traffic court, small claims, even probate depending on the complexity of the estate. However, beyond that, with no training, you are going to find yourself very quickly out of your element. There is a lot of procedure to court. Things just have to be done a certain way. Yes there are overarching rules that apply to all the courts, but there are also a bunch of little variances between jurisdictions. Thus, without familiarity with those procedures, you are going to have a very difficult time trying to make headway against an experienced attorney on the other side. Plus, you are most likely not going to be familiar with the judge, an experienced attorney will be. That attorney is going to know what that judge likes, doesn't like, and how to use that to his advantage.

Having said all that, it simply comes down to you are emotionally invested in the case. Even if one is an attorney, representing oneself is a bad idea. You are focused on seeing your side of the case, and it is very difficult to extract yourself from that. You need someone who will advocate for you, but can also keep a clear head about what the other side has going for/against it. Many people are convinced their case is black and white. It rarely is. It is almost always some shade of grey, and that's why you need somebody who can look at the whole picture.

You sound like a pretty good lawyer. There are so few out there. A good lawyer can also help a client steer clear of leading questions and enforce the virtue of silence. I'm not so sure about the advantage between a lawyer and Judge though. Actual forums, as in stuff like PHPBB tend to be far more balanced. I think the circle jerk we see in places like Reddit and on certain subs in Voat is almost exclusively a consequence of our voting system. The voting system inherently encourages circle jerks. Imagine there's something that 50% of a sub loves and 50% of a sub hates. If both sides vote equally, that content would end up at 0 points. It'd end up ranked below something that 1% of the sub likes, but 0% dislike. That's just pretty much stupid. You end up hiding content that 50% of a sub likes. Let's not even get into content that 40% like but 60% dislike - that content is dead and buried. Why exactly do people support this voting system again...?

There's also the issue of /new watchers. Most people don't like digging through /new. Those that are willing to waste their time doing so have an enormous amount of control over the content everybody else gets to see. A quick downvote for instance is generally enough to ensure content remains seen by almost no users.

There's a lot of alternatives to these voting systems, but no site yet seems interesting in trying them out. Probably because regardless of the results, it'd end up pissing off some decent chunk of your userbase.
